unit.title: Variation and Inheritance
unit.blurb: Chromosomes, genes and DNA, how sex is inherited, how a fetus develops, inherited and environmental variation, natural selection and what changes population size.

O1.t: Describe chromosomes, genes and DNA and how scientists worked out DNA's structure.

O2.t: Describe fertilisation and explain how sex is determined by X and Y chromosomes.

O3.t: Describe how a fetus develops and how the mother's health affects it.

O5.t: Explain natural selection, including antibiotic and insecticide resistance.

O6.t: Describe how environmental changes, including human activity, affect populations and can cause extinction.

captions: Welcome to Camday.
This lesson was written by the Camday teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 3: Variation and Inheritance.
Malaria, spread by mosquitoes, kills more than half a million people a year.
Insecticide-treated bed nets protect sleepers, but they have become less effective over time.
Why? By the end of this unit, you'll know.
Inside the nucleus of every cell are chromosomes,
carrying the genetic information that controls the cell.
Each species has a set number: humans have 23 pairs, 46 in all,
including one pair of sex chromosomes.
Camels have 74, and fruit flies just 8!
Each chromosome carries hundreds or thousands of genes.
A gene is a section of DNA that controls a characteristic, or trait,
such as eye colour.
Genes can have different forms: one form may give a cat long fur,
another short fur.
Chromosomes are made of DNA and proteins.
A DNA molecule has two strands twisted like a ladder: a double helix.
When cells divide, the chromosomes are copied,
so each new cell gets a complete set.
Scientists found DNA long before they understood it.
In 1869, Friedrich Miescher found a substance he called nuclein.
Albrecht Kossel named DNA and RNA, and Phoebus Levene discovered DNA's building blocks.
In 1944, Avery, MacLeod and McCarty showed that DNA, not protein,
carries hereditary information. Then in 1953, James Watson
and Francis Crick discovered the double helix structure.
Their model relied on Rosalind Franklin's X-ray images:
science develops as people build on each other's work.
In 2003, the Human Genome Project mapped all human genes,
helping to find genes behind disorders like cystic fibrosis.

captions: Every egg carries an X chromosome.
A sperm carries either an X or a Y.
We model this by tossing a coin 100 times:
heads for an X sperm, tails for a Y sperm.
Predict: how many of the 100 'babies' will be girls?
Pause and decide.
Watch. After 20 tosses, there are 11 girls and 9 boys.
After 100 tosses, there are 48 girls and 52 boys:
very close to half each.
Explain what you saw.
Half of all sperm carry an X and half carry a Y,
so each baby has an equal chance of being XX, a girl,
or XY, a boy.
Small samples can be uneven,
but with many tosses the result gets close to half and half.
The father's sperm decides the sex.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Inheritance is the passing of traits from parents to offspring.
Sperm and egg cells have only 23 chromosomes each.
At fertilisation their nuclei fuse,
making a zygote with all 46 and a unique combination of DNA.
One pair of chromosomes decides sex: females are XX and males are XY.
Every egg carries an X,
but a sperm can carry an X or a Y.
So the father's sperm decides: X makes a girl, Y makes a boy,
about fifty-fifty.
The zygote divides into a ball of cells,
which implants in the uterus wall.
It's called an embryo until about nine weeks, then a fetus.
If one zygote splits in two, we get identical twins;
two separate eggs give non-identical twins.
The fetus grows in the uterus for about 40 weeks.
The placenta passes oxygen,
nutrients and antibodies from the mother and takes away wastes.
The umbilical cord connects them,
and the amnion and its fluid cushion the fetus.
Harmful substances also cross the placenta, especially in the first weeks,
when organs form. A balanced diet with folic acid, iron and calcium is vital.
Smoking, alcohol and drugs can cause birth defects, low birth weight or miscarriage.
